(ICSE 2013) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: developers avoid static-analysis tools when warnings are noisy, hard to interpret or poorly integrated into their workflow — https://www.researchgate.net/publication/261192385_Why_don't_software_developers_use_static_analysis_tools_to_find_bugs

Vassallo, Panichella, Palomba, Proksch, Gall, Zaidman, 'How developers engage with static analysis tools in different contexts' (EMSE 25, 2020) — relayed by the orchestrator's search — https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10664-019-09750-5

'An empirical study of suppressed static analysis warnings' (PACMSE / FSE 2025, DOI 10.1145/3715729) and 'Quieting the static: a study of static analysis alert suppressions' (arXiv:2311.07482) — relayed by the orchestrator's search (titles confirmed) — https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3715729 and https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.07482

Trautsch, Herbold, Grabowski, 'A longitudinal study of static analysis warning evolution and the effects of PMD on software quality in Apache open source projects' (EMSE 2020; arXiv:1912.02179) — relayed by the orchestrator's search — https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.02179
notes: Owns the hygiene of the build and its checks as one change meets them: a change leaves the build free of new compiler and analyzer warnings, a suppression is scoped to the narrowest construct and carries its reason, a blanket or unused suppression is removed, the project's configured analyzers and tests run before the change is proposed, a strictness setting is not weakened to make a change pass, and a failing or flaky check is fixed or reported rather than skipped. Yields the defect a given analyzer rule reports to the topic that owns that defect, formatter and style conventions to layout-and-coding-style, dependency declarations and versions to dependency-management, and test quality to the tests group. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust: a card names 'the project's configured analyzer' and 'the language's suppression mechanism', never one tool, and a rule that holds in one language belongs to a language-specific corpus. The design of CI and delivery pipelines, release and deployment process, and team policy on tooling are process and team management and stay outside the corpus.

notes: Owns the dependencies a change adds, keeps or removes: whether a new dependency is warranted against what it costs transitively, declaring every dependency the code imports directly rather than relying on a transitive one, version constraints and a committed lock file for reproducible resolution, removing a declared dependency the code no longer uses, and moving off a version with a known vulnerability. Yields a library's own compatibility promises, breaking changes and deprecation to api-evolution-and-deprecation, which shares SEG21; build and check hygiene to build-warnings-static-analysis-ci; and validation of untrusted input to security-hygiene-in-ordinary-code. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust: a card names 'the ecosystem's manifest and lock file', never one package manager, and a rule that holds in one ecosystem belongs to a language-specific corpus. Supply-chain security design beyond the hygiene of one change is security-critical design, a reserved specialty, and an organization's dependency policy (a one-version rule, approval of new dependencies) is process and team management, outside the corpus.

Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust: a card names 'the environment, a flag or a configuration file', never one library, and a rule that holds in one language belongs to a language-specific corpus. Distributed configuration services and dynamic configuration pushed across a fleet are distributed systems, and feature-flag rollout policy is process and team management; both stay outside the corpus.

notes: Owns text and locale at the code level: an explicit encoding at every boundary where bytes become text or text becomes bytes (files, network, processes) rather than the platform default, an explicit locale for locale-sensitive operations (case mapping, number and date formatting, collation) and a locale-independent one for machine-readable text, user-visible strings kept out of code for translation and never assembled from translated fragments, length and indexing by the unit the operation means (bytes, code points or user-perceived characters), normalization before comparing text, timestamps stored as instants and converted to a time zone only at display, and invisible or bidirectional control characters in source text. Yields which values are configuration to runtime-configuration, the parsing of text formats to parsing-and-grammar-based-input, and normalization done as part of validating untrusted input to security-hygiene-in-ordinary-code. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust: a card names 'the language's explicit-encoding or explicit-locale API', never one library, and a rule that holds in one language belongs to a language-specific corpus. Which languages and regions a product supports and the content of its translations are product or UX decisions, and platform-specific text handling is cross-platform construction; both stay outside the corpus.

Yields writing code that is easy to read to the code-group topics (naming-identifiers, control-flow, comments-and-self-documenting-code); the reviewer's reading of a proposed change to code-review-as-author-and-reviewer; pinning current behaviour with tests to seams-and-characterization-tests; and localizing an observed failure to debugging. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a rule that holds in one language belongs to a language-specific corpus. Yields the size and shape of one change to small-steps-and-minimal-diffs; comment content in the source to comments-and-self-documenting-code; and each defect a reviewer looks for to the topic that owns that defect. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust and across review tools; a rule that holds in one language belongs to a language-specific corpus. Review policy (who must approve, ownership and readability approvals, reviewer assignment, turnaround targets) is process and team management and stays outside the corpus.

Bratus, Locasto, Patterson, Sassaman, Shubina, 'Exploit programming: from buffer overflows to weird machines and theory of computation' (;login: 2011) and Poll, 'LangSec revisited: input security flaws of the second kind' (LangSec 2018) — formulation and reception of the input-handling discipline; the evidence layer rests on CWE-20 Improper Input Validation, CWE-1286 and the OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (OWASP/CheatSheetSeries cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.md, fetched)
notes: Owns the structure of input: a real parser for a structured format (JSON, CSV, XML, URLs, dates, a configuration or query language) instead of splitting or matching by hand, stating the accepted grammar or format explicitly, parsing once at the edge into a typed representation and working on that rather than re-checking raw strings, rejecting malformed input as a whole with a precise error instead of partial processing, regular expressions bounded against catastrophic backtracking and anchored to what they mean, and fuzz or round-trip tests of a parser. Yields whether a well-formed value crossing a trust boundary is acceptable (allow-lists, injection, unsafe deserialization of untrusted data) to security-hygiene-in-ordinary-code; preconditions inside the boundary to defensive-programming; generators for parser tests to property-based-testing; decoding bytes into text to internationalization-and-text-encoding; and state machines for lexers to table-driven-and-state-machines. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust: a card names 'the language's standard or established parser for the format', never one library, and a rule that holds in one language belongs to a language-specific corpus. Hardening a parser against a determined adversary and designing a protocol are security-critical design, and parsing theory and parser-generator research are algorithm research; both are reserved specialties the cards do not enter.

notes: Owns validation of a value that crosses a trust boundary (type, length, range and allow-list at the point of entry) and the hygiene every ordinary change owes: parameterized queries and argument vectors instead of SQL or shell commands built from strings, output encoding for the context the value is written into, no evaluation of untrusted input as code, no secret in code, tests or version control, least privilege in what the code asks for (scopes, permissions, file modes), secure defaults, and a vetted library primitive rather than a hand-written one. Yields preconditions and fail-fast inside the trust boundary to defensive-programming; the structure of input and the choice of parser to parsing-and-grammar-based-input; updating a vulnerable dependency to dependency-management; how configuration is supplied to runtime-configuration; and log content and levels to logging-and-diagnostic-output. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust: a card names 'the driver's parameter binding' or 'the template engine's contextual escaping', never one library, and a rule that holds in one language belongs to a language-specific corpus. Security-critical design (threat modelling, authentication and authorization schemes, cryptographic and protocol design) is a reserved specialty: the cards stop at the hygiene above, with the OWASP cheat sheets, ASVS and CWE as the standards layer, and the agent names the specialty and stops.
